sentences.text: The Bodmer Lab is a digital library of world literature from the Bodmer collection, organized in 'constellations', one of them the Bodmer Papyri (Revelation First census record), "Une bibliothèque numérique de la littérature mondiale" in its own words (the Lab's home page), and a hub for research and digitisation born of a partnership of the University of Geneva and the Martin Bodmer Foundation that "has made a significant number of these rare and fragile documents available to the public" (the Lab's About page).

The home page names the partners as "la Faculté des lettres de l'Université de Genève et la Fondation Martin Bodmer" (home page), the census records that partnership as the operator, the site at bodmerlab.unige.ch, and the Bodmer Papyri constellation and the Fondation Martin Bodmer among the entity's other names (census record), and a third-party page on the card rail is titled "The Bodmer Lab, a Digital Library" (Storience card).

The About page states that the Lab is "Supported by the Fondation Ernst and Lucie Schmidheiny" and grew "thanks to the exceptional support" of that foundation, and lists its direction as Michel Jeanneret (1940-2019), Radu Suciu and Jérôme David (the About page).

The Fondation Martin Bodmer defines itself as at once a heritage library inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World programme, a place of research and conservation, and a museum open to all "dédié à l'écrit, des origines de l'écriture jusqu'à nos jours", whose heritage library "est accessible exclusivement aux chercheurs" (the Fondation's home page); Wikipedia calls it "a library and museum specialised in manuscripts and precious editions" in Cologny, just outside Geneva, holding some 160,000 items, Sumerian clay tablets and Greek papyri among them (Wikipedia, 'Bodmer Library').

The About page describes the Foundation's collection as "inscriptions, manuscripts and printed documents, from the oldest examples of writing up through the present day", the Fondation invites visitors on a journey through "cinq millénaires d'histoire de l'écrit" (About page; the Fondation's home page), and the census places the entity's coverage at the Bibliotheca Bodmeriana, Cologny, with no period stated for the papyri (census record).

Its dates stand two ways: the Fondation's page gives "Bibliothèque fondée en 1951" and "Fondation Martin Bodmer créée en 1971" (the Fondation's home page), while Wikipedia says that Martin Bodmer "established the library in the 1920s" and that the Foundation was established "In 1970, shortly before Bodmer's death", to make the collection accessible and conserve it (Wikipedia, 'Bodmer Library').

The Lab takes its principle from the collector: the Bibliotheca Bodmeriana "was conceived by Martin Bodmer as a 'library of world literature'", and the Lab decided "to take this intellectual ambition seriously and make it the guiding principle of the Bodmer Lab", using new technology to bring out that library's structure (About page), a library Bodmer built, Wikipedia says, around what he saw as the five pillars of world literature, the Bible, Homer, Dante, Shakespeare and Goethe (Wikipedia, 'Bodmer Library').

The home page sets the Lab the equation "comment valoriser une collection privée exceptionnelle en tenant compte de son projet intellectuel d'ensemble et avec l'appui des nouvelles technologies ?" and gives its tools the end of re-inscribing the digitized documents "dans leur époque et, plus largement, dans cette « bibliothèque de la littérature mondiale » dont rêvait Martin Bodmer" (home page); the Capture Registry records that this end of the record is not carried at the name (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The lineage is Martin Bodmer's: an essay by Jérôme David presented on the home page holds that Bodmer first conceived the collection "comme une histoire de l'esprit humain sur quatre millénaires" and, from Hitler's coming to power, as one of the only possible refuges of a humanism preserved from Nazi myths (home page), and the Capture Registry finds that at the name "'Martin Bodmer' appears only inside the partner's name, never as the collection or vision the library comes from" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The census gives the method as digitization and online cataloguing of the Bodmer collection (census record); the Lab states its own terms: it has prioritised the materiality of the works, with OCR planned "later rather than sooner" so that "the texts come into view through the lens of their editorial editions", it does not digitise the collection whole, since "Exhaustiveness can actually be misleading when put into practice", and data joined to commentary on their cultural significance are what it calls "smart data" (About page).

Its constellations are subsets of Martin Bodmer's collection "choisis pour leur intérêt et leur rareté" (home page), approached as "partially autonomous and requiring specific subject knowledge" and each entrusted to internationally recognised specialists, and the Lab also speaks to "a wider audience, schoolchildren, explorers and lovers of learning" through videos, image libraries, digital stories and games (About page).

The Bodmer Papyri constellation is an "Online catalog of the papyrus and parchment manuscripts in the Bodmer collection" (the constellation's page) whose aim is "to produce a detailed, online catalog of the papyrus and parchment manuscripts at the Fondation Martin Bodmer" (home page); the census takes as its unit a digitized document, for the papyri a papyrus or parchment manuscript of the Fondation, as its text object those manuscripts among the collection's literature, and as its finding that aim (census record).

The home page counts "56 documents numérisés" in the constellation and its catalogue lists 56 manuscripts and no prints (home page; the constellation's page), the census's count as of 2026-10-30 (census record), while Wikipedia's hatnote points to "a list of the 58 papyri in Bodmer's collection" (Wikipedia, 'Dishna Papers').

The catalogue numbers each manuscript with "PB (Papyrus Bodmer) and an Arabic number or a Latin letter", in most cases matching the older Roman numerals ("P.Bodmer II = PB 2"), under Daniel Sharp of Brigham Young University, Hawaii, and Brent Nongbri of the MF Norwegian School of Theology, Religion, and Society (the constellation's page), for papyri which, "more than two thousand years old", the Lab says "require different technological treatment" from nineteenth-century editions (About page).

Most of these manuscripts were acquired by Martin Bodmer in the 1950s and early 1960s, and many "seem to have formed part of a larger ancient collection" in Greek, Coptic and Latin, of which only Greek and Coptic are in the Bodmer collection (the constellation's page); Wikipedia gives them as the Dishna Papers, "also often known as the Bodmer Papyri", twenty-two papyri found at Dishna, Egypt, in 1952 and bought by Martin Bodmer, held now also at the Vatican, Oslo, Barcelona and elsewhere, so that many scholars have preferred the name Dishna Papers since the mid-2010s, and reports Lundhaug's argument (2018) that they came from the same monastic library as the Nag Hammadi codices (Wikipedia, 'Dishna Papers').

They mix Christian and classical books: PB 3, a codex of the Gospel According to John and part of Genesis in Coptic; PB M, the Menander codex; PB T, parts of Daniel in Greek with book 6 of Thucydides (the constellation's page), and the census holds the entity "NOT a papyrus database: the papyri are one constellation of a library of world literature" (census record).

The constellation's page calls these manuscripts "highly important for the history of early Christianity" and, for their preservation, of exceptional interest to historians of the book (the constellation's page); Wikipedia says that some of them "are among the oldest remaining copies of the New Testament" and that the first manuscript was bought in 1956, Papyrus Bodmer II, P66 (Wikipedia, 'Bodmer Library').

Wikipedia dates the oldest, P66, a text of the Gospel of John in the Alexandrian text-type, to about 200 AD, among papyri of the Old and New Testaments, early Christian literature, Homer and Menander; names P72 the earliest known copy of Jude and 1 and 2 Peter, P75 a partial codex of most of Luke and John acquired by the Vatican Library in 2007, and P74, the latest, of the sixth or seventh century, with P66, P73 and P74 among the library's items; and reports Floyd V. Filson's conclusion from the two Bodmer texts of John and the Chester Beatty Papyri that "there was no uniform text of the Gospels in Egypt in the third century" (Wikipedia, 'Dishna Papers'; 'Bodmer Library').

The census asks of every resource in its field "What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?", places the Bodmer Lab in the intersection of papyrology and textual discovery, "manuscripts, editions, new finds and redatings", and states its correction, "Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early": the priority thesis, not the old early date (census record).

Its worked question asks "Which papyri bear on the date of Revelation, and how is each one dated?", because "A papyrus dates its copy, and the composition must come before it" and most early New Testament papyri are dated by handwriting alone; it names the entity there as "the Bodmer papyri catalogue, in production", and records the gap that no record in its batch gives a sourced date and dating method for P47 or the other papyri of Revelation (census record).

The census's reading of the entity is the papyrological inversion: "the Bodmer papyri include some of the earliest New Testament papyri. The saved pages do not name them; the bearing is the archive's reading, to be checked against the catalogue" (census record); in the field, Wikipedia names P66, P72 and P75 among them, and the constellation's page names PB 3, a Coptic John (Wikipedia, 'Dishna Papers'; the constellation's page).

The inversion is #202's third claim: "The earliest physical NT witness is Johannine (𝔓52, commonly dated c. 125 CE), not Pauline (𝔓46, usually dated c. 175–225 CE)", the earliest physical copy of the Apocalypse, 𝔓98, predates the earliest physical copy of Romans, and "Papyrological dates are ranges, not certainties" (#202); the work plan sets out the same "papyrological receipts, in chronological order of earliest physical copy", and reads them as an epistemic inversion, the Pauline dating treated as ironclad though "its earliest physical witness is a codex from the turn of the third century" (#1217, first in #832).

The archive's earliest statement on the class, in the Space Ark, holds that "Revelation is among the earliest NT texts preserved in manuscript fragments (P18, P47, P98), contemporaneous with or preceding fragments of John and Paul" and that "The textual record does not contradict first-composition" (#636); the Bodmer papyri of John that the field dates, P66 at about 200 AD and P75, stand among the fragments of John that comparison names (Wikipedia, 'Dishna Papers').

The archive states the limit with the claim, "The section does not argue that papyrological dating of copies establishes composition dates" (#1217), and #202 is falsified if "a document in the NT can be securely dated earlier than any plausible date for Revelation" (#202); the census holds that the entity answers which Bodmer papyri are digitized and catalogued online and does not answer "the dates or contents of particular papyri (catalogue entries not opened)", its saved pages stating no limits (census record).

The census names the entity again in its question "Which manuscripts can be seen directly online, and which only through an edition?", as "digitized Bodmer papyri", with evidence of the kinds manuscript images and catalogue or metadata and data access through an online catalogue and images it did not open (census record); the archive frames the class as a field in which digital libraries are evaluated by "collections, discovery, preservation and services evaluated as connected functions" (#1680).

Unless otherwise stated the site's contents are published "sous une licence Creative commons CC-BY-NC, 4.0" (home page), as the census records, which also records the entity as active, the papyri constellation described as in production, and the catalogue entries and the Fondation's collection pages as unchecked (census record).

On Google AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-31, the name was set out as three entities, "the humanities library first", and the user asked which was meant (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), the library held first as "A research and digitization project partnering the University of Geneva, the Martin Bodmer Foundation" with "the Bodmer Papyri (early Christian and classical texts)" and its two homonyms beside it as distinct, so that the registry reads it "same, not collision" and finds "A shared name is resolved honestly, by listing and asking" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; census record).

Its analysis: "what the field comes for, the papyri of John and Luke among them, is one parenthesis, and the shorter address belongs on the web to a laboratory of fly hearts"; the two cards headed bodmerlab.org are Rolf Bodmer's Drosophila laboratory, the papyri's count and aim are not composed and their catalogue arrives only on a card, neither homonym is bound to the target, the record was built the day before and no card cites it, and the dimensional PER is 0.267 (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

sentences.text: The Bodmer Lab is "Une bibliothèque numérique de la littérature mondiale", a research and digitisation project of a partnership between the Faculty of Letters of the University of Geneva and the Fondation Martin Bodmer, which has made a significant number of the collection's rare and fragile documents public (home page; About page).

It is supported by the Fondation Ernst and Lucie Schmidheiny, directed by Michel Jeanneret (1940-2019), Radu Suciu and Jérôme David, and titled by a third-party page "The Bodmer Lab, a Digital Library" (About page; Storience card).

Its partner, the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, is a heritage library on UNESCO's Memory of the World programme, open to researchers only, a place of research and conservation and a museum of writing across five millennia, holding inscriptions, manuscripts and printed documents, some 160,000 items (the Fondation's page; About page; Wikipedia).
The Fondation's page gives the library as founded in 1951 and the Fondation as created in 1971; Wikipedia gives the library as established in the 1920s and the Foundation in 1970.

The Lab's guiding principle is Martin Bodmer's conception of his collection as a "library of world literature", built on five pillars, whose structure it uses new technology to bring out (About page; Wikipedia).

It sets itself the problem of valorising an exceptional private collection with its intellectual project, re-inscribing the documents in their time and in Bodmer's library of world literature, which Jérôme David traces to a history of the human spirit and a refuge from Nazi myths (home page).
It prioritises the materiality of the works over OCR, digitises by selection rather than exhaustively, and joins its data to commentary as "smart data" (About page).

Its constellations are partially autonomous subsets of the collection chosen for interest and rarity, each supervised by specialists, and it addresses a wider public through videos and games (About page; home page).

The Bodmer Papyri constellation is an online catalogue of the papyrus and parchment manuscripts of the Fondation, with 56 manuscripts digitised, numbered PB after the older P.Bodmer numerals, supervised by Daniel Sharp and Brent Nongbri, the papyri requiring their own technological treatment (constellation page; home page; About page).

L_BA.text: The Bodmer Lab is a digital library of world literature from the Bodmer collection, organized in 'constellations', one of them the Bodmer Papyri (Revelation First census record), "Une bibliothèque numérique de la littérature mondiale" in its own words (the Lab's home page), and a hub for research and digitisation born of a partnership of the University of Geneva and the Martin Bodmer Foundation that "has made a significant number of these rare and fragile documents available to the public" (the Lab's About page). The home page names the partners as "la Faculté des lettres de l'Université de Genève et la Fondation Martin Bodmer" (home page), the census records that partnership as the operator, the site at bodmerlab.unige.ch, and the Bodmer Papyri constellation and the Fondation Martin Bodmer among the entity's other names (census record), and a third-party page on the card rail is titled "The Bodmer Lab, a Digital Library" (Storience card). The About page states that the Lab is "Supported by the Fondation Ernst and Lucie Schmidheiny" and grew "thanks to the exceptional support" of that foundation, and lists its direction as Michel Jeanneret (1940-2019), Radu Suciu and Jérôme David (the About page). The Fondation Martin Bodmer defines itself as at once a heritage library inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World programme, a place of research and conservation, and a museum open to all "dédié à l'écrit, des origines de l'écriture jusqu'à nos jours", whose heritage library "est accessible exclusivement aux chercheurs" (the Fondation's home page); Wikipedia calls it "a library and museum specialised in manuscripts and precious editions" in Cologny, just outside Geneva, holding some 160,000 items, Sumerian clay tablets and Greek papyri among them (Wikipedia, 'Bodmer Library'). The About page describes the Foundation's collection as "inscriptions, manuscripts and printed documents, from the oldest examples of writing up through the present day", the Fondation invites visitors on a journey through "cinq millénaires d'histoire de l'écrit" (About page; the Fondation's home page), and the census places the entity's coverage at the Bibliotheca Bodmeriana, Cologny, with no period stated for the papyri (census record). Its dates stand two ways: the Fondation's page gives "Bibliothèque fondée en 1951" and "Fondation Martin Bodmer créée en 1971" (the Fondation's home page), while Wikipedia says that Martin Bodmer "established the library in the 1920s" and that the Foundation was established "In 1970, shortly before Bodmer's death", to make the collection accessible and conserve it (Wikipedia, 'Bodmer Library'). The Lab takes its principle from the collector: the Bibliotheca Bodmeriana "was conceived by Martin Bodmer as a 'library of world literature'", and the Lab decided "to take this intellectual ambition seriously and make it the guiding principle of the Bodmer Lab", using new technology to bring out that library's structure (About page), a library Bodmer built, Wikipedia says, around what he saw as the five pillars of world literature, the Bible, Homer, Dante, Shakespeare and Goethe (Wikipedia, 'Bodmer Library'). The home page sets the Lab the equation "comment valoriser une collection privée exceptionnelle en tenant compte de son projet intellectuel d'ensemble et avec l'appui des nouvelles technologies ?" and gives its tools the end of re-inscribing the digitized documents "dans leur époque et, plus largement, dans cette « bibliothèque de la littérature mondiale » dont rêvait Martin Bodmer" (home page); the Capture Registry records that this end of the record is not carried at the name (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The lineage is Martin Bodmer's: an essay by Jérôme David presented on the home page holds that Bodmer first conceived the collection "comme une histoire de l'esprit humain sur quatre millénaires" and, from Hitler's coming to power, as one of the only possible refuges of a humanism preserved from Nazi myths (home page), and the Capture Registry finds that at the name "'Martin Bodmer' appears only inside the partner's name, never as the collection or vision the library comes from" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The census gives the method as digitization and online cataloguing of the Bodmer collection (census record); the Lab states its own terms: it has prioritised the materiality of the works, with OCR planned "later rather than sooner" so that "the texts come into view through the lens of their editorial editions", it does not digitise the collection whole, since "Exhaustiveness can actually be misleading when put into practice", and data joined to commentary on their cultural significance are what it calls "smart data" (About page). Its constellations are subsets of Martin Bodmer's collection "choisis pour leur intérêt et leur rareté" (home page), approached as "partially autonomous and requiring specific subject knowledge" and each entrusted to internationally recognised specialists, and the Lab also speaks to "a wider audience, schoolchildren, explorers and lovers of learning" through videos, image libraries, digital stories and games (About page). The Bodmer Papyri constellation is an "Online catalog of the papyrus and parchment manuscripts in the Bodmer collection" (the constellation's page) whose aim is "to produce a detailed, online catalog of the papyrus and parchment manuscripts at the Fondation Martin Bodmer" (home page); the census takes as its unit a digitized document, for the papyri a papyrus or parchment manuscript of the Fondation, as its text object those manuscripts among the collection's literature, and as its finding that aim (census record). The home page counts "56 documents numérisés" in the constellation and its catalogue lists 56 manuscripts and no prints (home page; the constellation's page), the census's count as of 2026-10-30 (census record), while Wikipedia's hatnote points to "a list of the 58 papyri in Bodmer's collection" (Wikipedia, 'Dishna Papers'). The catalogue numbers each manuscript with "PB (Papyrus Bodmer) and an Arabic number or a Latin letter", in most cases matching the older Roman numerals ("P.Bodmer II = PB 2"), under Daniel Sharp of Brigham Young University, Hawaii, and Brent Nongbri of the MF Norwegian School of Theology, Religion, and Society (the constellation's page), for papyri which, "more than two thousand years old", the Lab says "require different technological treatment" from nineteenth-century editions (About page). Most of these manuscripts were acquired by Martin Bodmer in the 1950s and early 1960s, and many "seem to have formed part of a larger ancient collection" in Greek, Coptic and Latin, of which only Greek and Coptic are in the Bodmer collection (the constellation's page); Wikipedia gives them as the Dishna Papers, "also often known as the Bodmer Papyri", twenty-two papyri found at Dishna, Egypt, in 1952 and bought by Martin Bodmer, held now also at the Vatican, Oslo, Barcelona and elsewhere, so that many scholars have preferred the name Dishna Papers since the mid-2010s, and reports Lundhaug's argument (2018) that they came from the same monastic library as the Nag Hammadi codices (Wikipedia, 'Dishna Papers'). They mix Christian and classical books: PB 3, a codex of the Gospel According to John and part of Genesis in Coptic; PB M, the Menander codex; PB T, parts of Daniel in Greek with book 6 of Thucydides (the constellation's page), and the census holds the entity "NOT a papyrus database: the papyri are one constellation of a library of world literature" (census record). The constellation's page calls these manuscripts "highly important for the history of early Christianity" and, for their preservation, of exceptional interest to historians of the book (the constellation's page); Wikipedia says that some of them "are among the oldest remaining copies of the New Testament" and that the first manuscript was bought in 1956, Papyrus Bodmer II, P66 (Wikipedia, 'Bodmer Library'). Wikipedia dates the oldest, P66, a text of the Gospel of John in the Alexandrian text-type, to about 200 AD, among papyri of the Old and New Testaments, early Christian literature, Homer and Menander; names P72 the earliest known copy of Jude and 1 and 2 Peter, P75 a partial codex of most of Luke and John acquired by the Vatican Library in 2007, and P74, the latest, of the sixth or seventh century, with P66, P73 and P74 among the library's items; and reports Floyd V. Filson's conclusion from the two Bodmer texts of John and the Chester Beatty Papyri that "there was no uniform text of the Gospels in Egypt in the third century" (Wikipedia, 'Dishna Papers'; 'Bodmer Library'). The census asks of every resource in its field "What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?", places the Bodmer Lab in the intersection of papyrology and textual discovery, "manuscripts, editions, new finds and redatings", and states its correction, "Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early": the priority thesis, not the old early date (census record). Its worked question asks "Which papyri bear on the date of Revelation, and how is each one dated?", because "A papyrus dates its copy, and the composition must come before it" and most early New Testament papyri are dated by handwriting alone; it names the entity there as "the Bodmer papyri catalogue, in production", and records the gap that no record in its batch gives a sourced date and dating method for P47 or the other papyri of Revelation (census record). The census's reading of the entity is the papyrological inversion: "the Bodmer papyri include some of the earliest New Testament papyri. The saved pages do not name them; the bearing is the archive's reading, to be checked against the catalogue" (census record); in the field, Wikipedia names P66, P72 and P75 among them, and the constellation's page names PB 3, a Coptic John (Wikipedia, 'Dishna Papers'; the constellation's page). The inversion is #202's third claim: "The earliest physical NT witness is Johannine (𝔓52, commonly dated c. 125 CE), not Pauline (𝔓46, usually dated c. 175–225 CE)", the earliest physical copy of the Apocalypse, 𝔓98, predates the earliest physical copy of Romans, and "Papyrological dates are ranges, not certainties" (#202); the work plan sets out the same "papyrological receipts, in chronological order of earliest physical copy", and reads them as an epistemic inversion, the Pauline dating treated as ironclad though "its earliest physical witness is a codex from the turn of the third century" (#1217, first in #832). The archive's earliest statement on the class, in the Space Ark, holds that "Revelation is among the earliest NT texts preserved in manuscript fragments (P18, P47, P98), contemporaneous with or preceding fragments of John and Paul" and that "The textual record does not contradict first-composition" (#636); the Bodmer papyri of John that the field dates, P66 at about 200 AD and P75, stand among the fragments of John that comparison names (Wikipedia, 'Dishna Papers'). The archive states the limit with the claim, "The section does not argue that papyrological dating of copies establishes composition dates" (#1217), and #202 is falsified if "a document in the NT can be securely dated earlier than any plausible date for Revelation" (#202); the census holds that the entity answers which Bodmer papyri are digitized and catalogued online and does not answer "the dates or contents of particular papyri (catalogue entries not opened)", its saved pages stating no limits (census record). The census names the entity again in its question "Which manuscripts can be seen directly online, and which only through an edition?", as "digitized Bodmer papyri", with evidence of the kinds manuscript images and catalogue or metadata and data access through an online catalogue and images it did not open (census record); the archive frames the class as a field in which digital libraries are evaluated by "collections, discovery, preservation and services evaluated as connected functions" (#1680). Unless otherwise stated the site's contents are published "sous une licence Creative commons CC-BY-NC, 4.0" (home page), as the census records, which also records the entity as active, the papyri constellation described as in production, and the catalogue entries and the Fondation's collection pages as unchecked (census record). On Google AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-31, the name was set out as three entities, "the humanities library first", and the user asked which was meant (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), the library held first as "A research and digitization project partnering the University of Geneva, the Martin Bodmer Foundation" with "the Bodmer Papyri (early Christian and classical texts)" and its two homonyms beside it as distinct, so that the registry reads it "same, not collision" and finds "A shared name is resolved honestly, by listing and asking" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; census record). The registry finds a third partner at the name, "the Fondation Ernst and Lucie Schmidheiny", not in the census's saved pages (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), the foundation the About page names as the Lab's supporter (About page); it finds that "'spanning 3,000 years' is a span the records do not state", that the licence is not carried, and that the composition names no person for the library and no identifier, with the library's About page the first card (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). Its analysis: "what the field comes for, the papyri of John and Luke among them, is one parenthesis, and the shorter address belongs on the web to a laboratory of fly hearts"; the two cards headed bodmerlab.org are Rolf Bodmer's Drosophila laboratory, the papyri's count and aim are not composed and their catalogue arrives only on a card, neither homonym is bound to the target, the record was built the day before and no card cites it, and the dimensional PER is 0.267 (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). Wikipedia has no article under 'Bodmer Lab' (Wikipedia, as fetched 2026-10-31), names "The Bodmer Lab" once, as the digitiser of the Foundation's First Folio of 1623 (Wikipedia, 'Bodmer Library'), and links the constellation as the "Bodmer Papyri Home Page" from the article to which 'Bodmer Papyri' redirects (Wikipedia, 'Dishna Papers').

case.statement: The archive reads the field's entity as the entity. The Revelation First census record describes the Bodmer Lab from its own home page, each field with its basis ('operator'), and answers for it the census's organizing question, what evidence a resource holds on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed; the capture record checks the composition at the name against those pages (CAP-1-04–CAP-1-07). No deposit names the Bodmer Lab, the Bodmer papyri or any of them. Four deposits bear on its classes: #202, #1217 and #636 apply the archive's papyrological inversion to the class of early New Testament papyri, with the limit that dating copies does not establish composition dates (#1217), and #1680 frames digital libraries as a field of connected functions. The census's own reading (rf_intersection), that the Bodmer papyri include some of the earliest New Testament papyri, takes the entity's holdings as the field gives them and adds their bearing on the dating question, to be checked against the catalogue. No defining record contests the field's ontology of the entity or supplies one the field lacks: ρ = extends, the equal-terms case (§0.9, §1.2a). The homonyms at the name, Rolf Bodmer's cardiovascular laboratory and Salford's Bodmer Laboratories, are distinct entities, set apart by the composition itself (CAP-1-16).

loci.quote: Papyrological inversion: the Bodmer papyri include some of the earliest New Testament papyri. The saved pages do not name them; the bearing is the archive's reading, to be checked against the catalogue.
The earliest physical NT witness is Johannine (𝔓52, commonly dated c. 125 CE), not Pauline (𝔓46, usually dated c. 175–225 CE).
The section does not argue that papyrological dating of copies establishes composition dates.
Revelation is among the earliest NT texts preserved in manuscript fragments (P18, P47, P98), contemporaneous with or preceding fragments of John and Paul.
The homonyms are set beside it as distinct, not merged with it, so the reading is same, not collision
